title: Monetary Policy Report – July 2018
summary: The Federal Reserve's July 2018 Monetary Policy Report documented a strong labor market in the first half of 2018, with nonfarm payrolls averaging 215,000 per month and the unemployment rate declining from 4.1% in December to 4.0% in June. The report noted that unemployment stood below all FOMC participants' estimates of the longer-run normal level and was close to lows last reached in 2000. The Fed also examined structural factors driving labor force participation trends, including the aging of the baby-boom generation and longer-run declines in prime-age participation rates.
key_points: Nonfarm payroll employment averaged 215,000 per month in H1 2018, up from the 2017 pace
Unemployment rate declined to 4.0% in June 2018, down from 4.1% in December 2017
The 4.0% unemployment rate is below all FOMC participants' estimates of the longer-run normal level and about 0.5 percentage point below the median estimate
Labor force participation rate (LFPR) was 62.9% in June, little changed on net since late 2013
Employment-to-population ratio reached 60.4% in June, gradually increasing since 2011
Job openings, quits rate, and hiring remain elevated; layoffs and initial unemployment claims near multi-decade lows
Aging population is a key contributor to the downward trend in overall LFPR, with 65+ share rising from 16% in 2000 to 19% in 2017, projected to reach 24% by 2026
Prime-age LFPRs have risen notably and consistently since 2013, driven by improving labor market conditions
why_it_matters: This semi-annual Monetary Policy Report provides the Federal Reserve's official assessment of economic conditions as of mid-2018, serving as the analytical foundation for FOMC policy decisions. The strong labor market data reported here informed expectations for continued gradual rate hikes through 2018. The deep examination of labor force participation trends—including demographic shifts, educational polarization, disability, caregiving, and opioid use factors—provides structural context that remains relevant for understanding post-pandemic labor supply dynamics.
macro_context: The report documented an economy with a labor market at or beyond full employment. Average payroll gains of 215,000/month were considerably faster than needed to absorb new labor force entrants. The unemployment rate at 4.0% was below all FOMC participants' longer-run estimates and roughly 0.5 pp below the median estimate. The employment-to-population ratio at 60.4% had been gradually increasing since 2011. These conditions indicated the Fed's dual mandate objectives were being achieved, supporting the policy normalization path in place at that time.
